# Imports
```{r}
# Load necessary libraries
library(dplyr)
library(GGally)
library(lsa)
library(tidyverse)
```

Create both one-way and two-way ANOVA. Use AIC to determine which one is better for the dataset.


```{r}
# Load data
travel_insurance_df <- read.csv("travel_insurance.csv")
names(travel_insurance_df)

# columns Agency,AgencyType,DistributionChannel,ProductName,Claim,Duration,Destination,NetSales,Commission,Gender,Age

# Assume travel_insurance_df is your full dataset

# Set a seed for reproducibility (optional)
set.seed(123)

# I have to limit this to 30% of the data because it won't work
# ! Note, when I switched to agency and product name, i was able to improve rendering times
subset_df <- travel_insurance_df[sample(nrow(travel_insurance_df), size = 0.95 * nrow(travel_insurance_df)), ]
```




```{r}
one_way_test <- aov(Commission ~ ProductName, data = subset_df)
two_way_test_with_ineraction <- aov(Commission ~ ProductName * AgencyType, data = subset_df)
two_way_test_without_ineraction <- aov(Commission ~ ProductName + AgencyType, data = subset_df)

summary(one_way_test)
summary(two_way_test_with_ineraction)
summary(two_way_test_without_ineraction)

AIC(one_way_test, two_way_test_with_ineraction, two_way_test_without_ineraction)




##                                 df      AIC
## one_way_test                    27 446808.6
## two_way_test_with_ineraction    29 446789.4
## two_way_test_without_ineraction 28 446792.6

# AIC comparison
cat("While two_way_test_with_ineraction had a lower AIC, the scores overall were fairly even. The more complex model (two_way_test_with_ineraction) was only slightly better than the same two way test without interaction")
```
